atoms.title: The bit — the unit of information
atoms.summary: One bit is the information in answering a single yes/no question whose two answers are equally likely.

depths.eli5: A bit is the answer to one yes-or-no question — the smallest possible piece of information. Think of guessing a number from 1 to 8. Ask 'is it 5 or higher?', then split what's left in half again, then again: three good yes/no questions always pin down the answer. Each answer is one bit, so the whole guess took three bits. 'Bit' is short for 'binary digit', meaning a single 0 or 1.
depths.core: Information is measured by how much it cuts down your uncertainty. The natural unit is the bit: the amount of information you gain from learning the result of a fair (50/50) coin flip. Picking one item out of 2^n equally likely options takes exactly n bits, because each yes/no answer halves the number of remaining possibilities. The mathematics uses the logarithm — the function that asks 'how many times must I halve N to reach 1?' — so identifying one item out of N equally likely items costs log2(N) bits.
depths.deep: The bit is dimensionless and logarithmic by necessity: information about independent events must add up, while the number of combined outcomes multiplies, and the logarithm is the unique function that turns products into sums. Using log base 2 fixes the unit as the bit; using the natural log (base e) gives 'nats', and base 10 gives 'dits' or 'hartleys' — the same quantity measured with a different ruler.

atoms.note: log2(N) bits identify one item out of N equally likely ones. Memorize: 10 bits ≈ a thousand, 20 bits ≈ a million, 30 bits ≈ a billion.

atoms.title: Probability distribution and expectation
atoms.summary: A distribution assigns nonnegative weights summing to one; expectation is the weighted average of outcomes.

depths.eli5: When different outcomes can happen, each with its own chance, the 'expectation' is the average result you'd get if you repeated the whole thing a huge number of times. For a fair six-sided die the outcomes 1 through 6 are equally likely, and their average is 3.5 — even though you can never actually roll a 3.5.
depths.core: A 'random variable' X is just a quantity whose value depends on chance (like a die roll). A 'probability distribution' lists each possible value x together with its probability p(x), where every p(x) is at least 0 and all of them add up to 1 (something must happen). The 'expectation' (or expected value, or mean) E[X] = Σ x p(x) is the probability-weighted average — the long-run average value. Expectation is 'linear': E[aX+bY] = aE[X]+bE[Y], and this holds even when X and Y influence each other. Almost every quantity in information theory turns out to be the expectation of some log-probability.
depths.deep: Linearity of expectation is the workhorse of algorithm analysis precisely because it needs no independence — you can sum per-element contributions regardless of how they correlate. 'Variance' (the spread around the mean), by contrast, does require care about covariance (how variables move together).

atoms.title: Shannon entropy
atoms.summary: Entropy is the average number of bits needed to describe an outcome — the exact amount of uncertainty in a distribution.

depths.eli5: Entropy measures how surprised you'll be, on average, by an outcome — and that surprise is exactly the amount of information the outcome carries. A coin that always lands heads has zero entropy: you already know the result, so learning it tells you nothing. A fair coin has one bit of entropy: each flip is a genuine 50/50 surprise. The more unpredictable something is, the higher its entropy.
depths.core: Shannon entropy H(X) = −Σ p(x) log2 p(x) is the average 'surprise' of an outcome, where the surprise of a single outcome with probability p is defined as −log2 p (rarer outcomes are more surprising). Measured in bits, entropy is the unique measure (up to a scaling choice) that is continuous, adds up for independent variables, and is largest for the uniform (all-equally-likely) distribution. It sets the absolute floor on lossless compression: on average you cannot encode X in fewer than H(X) bits per symbol. ('Lossless' means the original can be perfectly reconstructed.)
depths.deep: Surprise is −log2 p because rarer events carry more information, independent events' surprises must add (while their probabilities multiply), and the logarithm is the function that converts multiplication into addition. Entropy is maximized by the uniform distribution and is exactly zero when one outcome is certain. It is concave in p, which is why blending two distributions together never decreases uncertainty.

atoms.note: Joint and conditional entropy obey the chain rule H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y|X); conditioning never increases entropy: H(X|Y) ≤ H(X).

atoms.title: Source coding theorem (and Kraft inequality)
atoms.summary: Lossless codes can compress a source down to its entropy, and no further — entropy is the compression limit.

depths.eli5: When you turn symbols into strings of 0s and 1s (a 'code'), you can give short codes to the things that show up a lot and longer codes to rare things — that's the trick Morse code uses, giving the common letter 'e' a single dot. Doing this shrinks your messages on average. But there's a hard floor: no matter how clever you are, you can't squeeze a message below its entropy, on average.
depths.core: Shannon's source coding theorem says the shortest possible average codeword length for a source equals its entropy: H(X) ≤ L̄ < H(X)+1 bits per symbol, and the leftover gap shrinks to zero when you encode long blocks of symbols at once. A 'prefix code' is one where no codeword is the start of another, so a stream of bits can be decoded with no separators ('uniquely decodable' = the bits can only be read one way). The Kraft inequality, Σ 2^(−ℓ_i) ≤ 1 (summing over codeword lengths ℓ_i), says exactly which sets of codeword lengths can form such a code.
depths.deep: The best codeword lengths are ℓ_i ≈ −log2 p_i, so the length of a codeword equals the surprise of its symbol. Huffman coding finds the optimal code when lengths must be whole numbers; arithmetic coding gets within a hair of the entropy bound by escaping the whole-number constraint. Kraft's inequality is what forbids a 'free lunch': shortening one codeword forces you to lengthen others.

sources: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (facts)

quiz.prompt: What lower bound does the source coding theorem place on the average length of any lossless code?

atoms.title: Mutual information
atoms.summary: Mutual information is the number of bits one variable reveals about another — the reduction in uncertainty from observing it.

depths.eli5: Mutual information is how much learning one thing tells you about another. If knowing today's clouds makes you more sure whether it'll rain, clouds and rain share mutual information. If two things have nothing to do with each other — like a coin flip in Tokyo and one in Paris — their mutual information is zero.
depths.core: Mutual information I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) measures how many bits observing Y removes from your uncertainty about X (here H(X) is the entropy of X and H(X|Y) is the leftover entropy once Y is known). It is symmetric (Y tells you as much about X as X tells you about Y), never negative, and exactly zero when X and Y are 'independent' (unrelated — knowing one says nothing about the other). Equivalently it is the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the true joint distribution and the product of the separate distributions, a number measuring how far the two variables are from being independent.
depths.deep: I(X;Y) ≥ 0 follows from the convexity of KL divergence (Gibbs' inequality). The data-processing inequality says no clever post-processing of Y can increase the information it carries about X: if X→Y→Z form a 'Markov chain' (Z depends on X only through Y) then I(X;Z) ≤ I(X;Y). This is the formal reason you cannot manufacture information by computation alone.

atoms.note: Mutual information is the rate quantity behind channel capacity, feature selection, and the information bottleneck in deep learning.
sources: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (facts)
Wikipedia (facts): Mutual information; Data processing inequality

quiz.answer: Exactly when X and Y are statistically independent.

atoms.title: Channel capacity and the noisy-channel coding theorem
atoms.summary: Every noisy channel has a maximum reliable rate, the capacity C, below which error can be driven to zero and above which it cannot.

depths.eli5: A 'channel' is any link that carries a message but can scramble it — a phone line with static, a scratched disc, a radio signal through interference. Shannon showed every noisy channel has a top speed (its 'capacity'): below that speed you can encode cleverly enough to be understood with essentially zero errors; push past it and mistakes become unavoidable no matter how clever you are.
depths.core: The capacity of a channel is the largest mutual information you can achieve between its input X and output Y, by choosing the best possible input distribution: C = max over p(x) of I(X;Y). Shannon's noisy-channel coding theorem says any transmission rate R below C can be achieved with arbitrarily small error using long 'block codes' (encoding many symbols together), while any rate above C is stuck with errors that never go to zero. So reliable communication and the noise floor are captured by a single number, C.
depths.deep: The proof that good codes exist is 'non-constructive': it uses random codebooks and 'typical set' decoding to prove good codes must exist, without naming one. Closing the gap to capacity with explicit, efficiently decodable codes took decades — turbo codes, LDPC codes, and polar codes (the first family proven to reach capacity on symmetric channels) finally did it. Capacity also lets you separate the two coding jobs: compress your data down to its entropy first, then protect it up to capacity, independently.

atoms.note: For a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p, C = 1 − H(p) bits per use, where H(p) is the binary entropy function.

atoms.title: Error-correcting codes and Hamming distance
atoms.summary: By spreading codewords far apart in Hamming distance, a code can detect and correct a bounded number of bit errors.

depths.eli5: Suppose the only valid messages you allow are very different from one another. Then if a few bits get flipped by noise, the corrupted message is still closest to exactly one valid message — so you 'snap' it back to that one and recover the original. That is error correction: build in enough difference that small damage is fixable.
depths.core: A code maps each message to a longer 'codeword'. The 'Hamming distance' between two codewords is the number of bit positions where they differ; the smallest such distance over all pairs is d_min. A code can detect up to d_min − 1 flipped bits and correct up to t = ⌊(d_min − 1)/2⌋ of them, because any received word within t flips of a unique codeword decodes back to it. 'Linear codes' (Hamming, Reed–Solomon, LDPC) use algebra over finite number systems so that encoding and decoding stay fast.
depths.deep: Error-correcting coding is a sphere-packing problem in 'Hamming space': put non-overlapping balls of radius t around each codeword. The Hamming bound caps how many codewords fit; the Gilbert–Varshamov bound guarantees a minimum density always exists. Shannon's channel capacity is the asymptotic ceiling these combinatorial bounds approach. Reed–Solomon codes underlie CDs, QR codes, and deep-space links; LDPC and polar codes power modern wireless.

atoms.title: Kolmogorov complexity
atoms.summary: The complexity of a string is the length of the shortest program that prints it — the algorithmic, per-object version of information.

depths.eli5: Ask: how short can a recipe (a computer program) be that prints out exactly this string of symbols? The string 'ababab...ab' a million times has a tiny recipe ('print ab a million times'). But a million truly random coin-flip results has no recipe shorter than just writing the whole thing out. That shortest-recipe length is the string's Kolmogorov complexity — its true, per-object amount of information.
depths.core: K(x) is the length of the shortest program that, run on a fixed 'universal Turing machine' U (an idealized general-purpose computer; see the Turing machine atom), prints x and stops. Unlike Shannon entropy, which describes a whole probability distribution, K describes one single object. The 'invariance theorem' guarantees that switching to a different universal machine changes K by at most a fixed additive constant, so K is well-defined up to that constant. A string is called 'random' or 'incompressible' when K(x) ≈ |x|, meaning it has no description shorter than itself.
depths.deep: K is not computable: no algorithm can output K(x) for every x. Chaitin's theorem sharpens this — any consistent formal system can prove statements of the form 'K(x) > c' for only finitely many x, no matter how large the true complexities get. This is Gödel's incompleteness dressed in information-theoretic clothes. The expected Kolmogorov complexity of strings drawn from a computable distribution equals that distribution's Shannon entropy up to a constant, tying the two notions of information together.

atoms.note: Most strings are incompressible by a simple counting argument: there are 2^n strings of length n but fewer than 2^n programs shorter than n, so most strings have no short description.

atoms.title: Sets, functions, and relations
atoms.summary: Sets are collections; functions map each input to one output; relations are any set of input–output pairs — the vocabulary of all formal definitions.

depths.eli5: A 'set' is just a bag of distinct things (the set of vowels, the set of whole numbers). A 'function' is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input — like 'double it', which turns 3 into 6 and never into anything else. A 'relation' is looser: it can link one input to several things at once, like 'is a sibling of'.
depths.core: A set is an unordered collection of distinct elements. A function f: A→B assigns to each element of the input set A (the 'domain') exactly one element of the output set B (the 'codomain'). A 'relation' between A and B is any collection of input–output pairs, so every function is a relation but not every relation is a function. 'Cardinality' measures a set's size. A function is a 'bijection' (a perfect one-to-one pairing) when it is both 'injective' (no two inputs share an output) and 'surjective' (every output is used).
depths.deep: Whether a set is 'countable' or 'uncountable' hinges on bijection: a set is countable if its elements can be paired one-to-one with the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, …. Cantor's diagonal argument shows the real numbers (and the set of all possible languages over an alphabet) are uncountable, while the set of all computer programs is only countable — the seed of why most functions can never be computed.

atoms.title: Finite automata (DFA and NFA)
atoms.summary: A finite automaton is a machine with finitely many states that reads input symbol by symbol and accepts or rejects.

depths.eli5: Picture a board game with a few squares ('states'). You read a word one letter at a time, and each letter tells you which square to hop to next. One square is where you start; some squares are marked 'win'. If you land on a win-square after reading the whole word, the machine 'accepts' that word. That little hopping game is a finite automaton.
depths.core: A 'deterministic finite automaton' (DFA) has a finite set of states, a rule ('transition function') that moves it to exactly one next state for each input symbol, a designated start state, and a set of accepting ('win') states. A 'nondeterministic finite automaton' (NFA) is allowed to branch into several states at once (or get stuck with none) and accepts a word if any branch ends in an accept state. Despite the extra freedom, DFAs and NFAs recognize exactly the same family of patterns — the 'regular languages' (the patterns describable by a finite-state machine, equivalently by a regular expression).
depths.deep: The 'subset construction' converts any NFA with n states into an equivalent DFA with up to 2^n states, proving the two models are equally powerful while exposing an exponential blowup in state count. A finite automaton has no memory beyond which single state it is currently in, which is exactly why it cannot count without limit — the limitation the pumping lemma makes precise.

atoms.note: Regular expressions, DFAs, and NFAs are three faces of the same expressive power: the regular languages.

atoms.title: Regular languages and the pumping lemma
atoms.summary: Regular languages are exactly those recognized by finite automata; the pumping lemma proves some languages are not regular.

depths.eli5: A 'language' here just means a set of allowed words. Finite-memory machines can recognize lots of word-patterns, but they can't truly count, because they only remember which of a few states they're in. So a pattern like 'some number of A's followed by the exact same number of B's' is beyond them — and the 'pumping lemma' is a clever trick that proves it.
depths.core: A language is 'regular' exactly when some DFA recognizes it. The pumping lemma states that for any regular language there is a length p such that every accepted string of length ≥ p can be cut into three parts xyz — with the middle part y non-empty and sitting within the first p symbols — so that repeating that middle part any number of times, xy^i z, still gives a string in the language for every i ≥ 0. If no such p can possibly work for a language, that language is not regular. This is the standard tool for proving patterns like {0^n 1^n} (n zeros then n ones) lie outside the regular class.
depths.deep: The pumping lemma is really the pigeonhole principle applied to states: a long enough accepted string forces the automaton to revisit some state, creating a loop (the y part) that can be traversed any number of times. The lemma is a necessary but not sufficient condition for regularity, so a clean non-regularity proof must show the pumping condition fails for every possible way of cutting the string.

atoms.title: Context-free languages and grammars
atoms.summary: Context-free grammars generate nested, recursive structure (like balanced parentheses) that finite automata cannot.

depths.eli5: A 'grammar' is a set of build-rules for words. Context-free grammars allow rules like 'a sentence can contain a smaller sentence inside it', which lets you build nested structures — matching brackets ( [ { } ] ), arithmetic expressions, and the syntax of programming languages — the kind of nesting that plain finite-state machines cannot handle.
depths.core: A 'context-free grammar' (CFG) is a set of 'production rules', each rewriting a single 'nonterminal' symbol (a placeholder) into a string of 'terminals' (actual symbols) and other nonterminals. CFGs generate the 'context-free languages', which are recognized by 'pushdown automata' — finite automata equipped with a 'stack' (a last-in-first-out memory, like a stack of plates). The stack provides exactly the bounded-recursion memory needed for balanced nesting such as {0^n 1^n} (n zeros then n ones) and programming-language syntax.
depths.deep: There is a pumping lemma for context-free languages too — with two pumpable segments instead of one — and it proves that languages like {0^n 1^n 2^n} are not context-free. Parsing a CFG can be done in polynomial time (the CYK algorithm runs in O(n^3)); deterministic CFGs admit linear-time parsers, which is why real compilers restrict their grammars to the well-behaved LL and LR subclasses.

atoms.note: Pushdown automata = finite automaton + one stack. Adding a second stack (or a tape) jumps all the way to Turing-machine power.

atoms.title: The Chomsky hierarchy
atoms.summary: Languages stratify into four nested classes — regular ⊂ context-free ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂ recursively enumerable — each tied to a machine model.

depths.eli5: There's a ladder of grammar power. Each rung can describe more complicated patterns than the one below it, and each needs a more powerful kind of machine to recognize it — from simple state-hopping machines at the bottom up to fully general computers at the top.
depths.core: Noam Chomsky classified grammars into four types by power: Type 3 (regular, recognized by finite automata), Type 2 (context-free, recognized by pushdown automata), Type 1 (context-sensitive, recognized by 'linear-bounded automata' — Turing machines whose tape is limited to the input length), and Type 0 (recursively enumerable, recognized by full Turing machines). The corresponding language classes are strictly nested — each inclusion is proper — so adding the right kind of memory to a machine strictly increases what it can recognize.
depths.deep: The hierarchy is really a memory ladder: no memory (finite states) → one stack (pushdown) → a tape bounded by the input length (linear-bounded) → an unbounded tape (Turing machine). The jump from Type 1 to Type 0 is the jump from 'always halts' to 'may run forever': context-sensitive languages are 'decidable' (a machine always halts with a yes/no), while recursively enumerable languages are only 'semi-decidable' (it halts and says yes on yes-instances but may loop forever otherwise).

atoms.title: The Turing machine
atoms.summary: A Turing machine is a finite controller with an unbounded tape — the standard mathematical model of any computation.

depths.eli5: Picture an endlessly long paper strip divided into cells, and a little head sitting over one cell. Following a short table of rules, the head reads the symbol under it, writes a symbol, and steps one cell left or right — over and over. That's it. This almost absurdly simple device can compute anything any real computer can; it's the standard model of what 'computing' even means.
depths.core: A Turing machine has a finite set of internal 'states', a read/write 'head', and an infinitely long 'tape' of cells. At each step it reads the symbol under the head and, according to its 'transition rule', writes a symbol, moves the head one cell left or right, and switches state — halting when it reaches an accept or reject state. Despite this simplicity it can carry out any algorithm: its unbounded tape gives it the unlimited memory that finite automata and pushdown automata lack.
depths.deep: A 'universal Turing machine' takes the description of any other Turing machine plus an input and simulates it step by step — the theoretical basis of the stored-program computer (software running on general hardware). Variations (multiple tapes, nondeterministic branching, multiple tracks) all compute exactly the same functions as the basic single-tape model, differing only by a polynomial-time overhead. The model pins down 'computable' precisely enough that we can prove certain tasks are impossible for any computer.

atoms.note: All reasonable models of computation — lambda calculus, register machines, cellular automata, your laptop — compute exactly the same functions as the Turing machine.

atoms.title: The Church–Turing thesis
atoms.summary: Anything effectively computable by any mechanical procedure is computable by a Turing machine — the definition of 'computable'.

depths.eli5: Any honest, spelled-out, step-by-step method you could ever follow by hand — a recipe with no guessing or magic — can also be carried out by a Turing machine. So 'a computer can do it' and 'there's a definite procedure for it' end up meaning the same thing.
depths.core: The Church–Turing thesis claims that the everyday intuitive idea of an 'effective procedure' (a mechanical, finite, unambiguous recipe) matches exactly what Turing machines — and equivalently the lambda calculus, recursive functions, and every other model — can compute. It is not a theorem but a claim that fixes a definition, made compelling by the striking fact that every independently invented model of computation has turned out to compute the very same set of functions.
depths.deep: The thesis is empirical and conceptual rather than provable, because it equates a precise formal class with an informal human idea. The 'physical' or 'extended' Church–Turing thesis goes further, claiming nature itself can compute nothing a Turing machine cannot (its polynomial-time version is challenged by quantum computing, which may be faster but not more capable). 'Hypercomputation' models exist on paper but need physically impossible resources like infinite-precision real numbers or completed infinite processes.

atoms.title: Decidability and recognizability
atoms.summary: A problem is decidable if some machine always halts with the right yes/no answer; merely recognizable if it halts on the yes-instances.

depths.eli5: A problem is 'decidable' if there's a method that always finishes and gives you a definite yes or no. It's only 'recognizable' (a weaker property) if the method correctly says yes whenever the true answer is yes, but might run forever — never answering — when the true answer is no.
depths.core: A 'language' here is the set of inputs whose answer is yes. A language is 'decidable' (also called 'recursive') if some Turing machine halts on every input and correctly accepts or rejects it. It is 'recognizable' (also called 'recursively enumerable') if some machine halts and accepts on every yes-instance but is allowed to loop forever on no-instances. The key bridge: a language is decidable exactly when both it and its 'complement' (the set of no-instances) are recognizable.
depths.deep: Problems that are recognizable but not decidable are the heart of computability theory: the halting problem is recognizable (just run the machine — if it halts, accept) yet not decidable, and its complement is not even recognizable. This asymmetry — you can always confirm halting, but you can never, in general, confirm non-halting — is the source of most undecidability proofs, which proceed by 'reduction' (showing that solving the new problem would let you solve the halting problem).

atoms.art_prompt: two flowcharts — a decider that always reaches HALT, and a recognizer with one branch that loops forever on 'no' inputs

quiz.prompt: State the relationship between decidability and recognizability.
quiz.answer: A language is decidable iff both it and its complement are recognizable (recursively enumerable).

quiz.prompt: Why is the halting problem recognizable but not decidable?
quiz.answer: You can confirm a yes by simulating until it halts, but you can never be sure a non-halting machine won't eventually stop, so no machine decides it in all cases.

atoms.title: The halting problem
atoms.summary: No algorithm can decide, for every program and input, whether that program eventually halts — the foundational undecidability result.

depths.eli5: You can't build a perfect 'will-this-program-eventually-finish?' checker that works for every program. Here's the catch: if such a checker existed, you could build a sneaky program that asks the checker about itself and then deliberately does the opposite of whatever the checker predicts — finishing when it's told it'll loop, looping when it's told it'll finish. That's a contradiction, so no perfect checker can exist.
depths.core: The halting problem asks: given a program P and an input x, will P(x) eventually stop ('halt') or run forever? Turing proved no algorithm can answer this correctly for all inputs. The proof is by 'diagonalization': assume a perfect halting-decider H exists, then build a program D that halts exactly when H predicts it loops, and run D on its own description — forcing a self-contradiction. So halting is 'undecidable' (no always-correct decider), though it remains 'recognizable' (you can confirm halting by just running and waiting).
depths.deep: Halting is the canonical undecidable problem from which countless others are proven undecidable by 'reduction': if solving problem A would let you solve halting, then A must be undecidable too. Rice's theorem generalizes this: every nontrivial property of the function a program computes (its input/output behavior) is undecidable. Undecidability is therefore pervasive, not some rare exotic case.

atoms.note: Rice's theorem: any nontrivial property of the language a program computes is undecidable — 'does this program ever output 42?' has no general algorithm.

atoms.title: Asymptotic notation (big-O)
atoms.equation: f(n)=O(g(n))\iff \exists c,n_0:\ f(n)\le c\,g(n)\ \forall n\ge n_0
atoms.summary: Big-O captures how a cost grows with input size, ignoring constants and small inputs — the language of efficiency.

depths.eli5: When we judge an algorithm, we care how its work grows as the problem gets bigger — not the exact number of seconds, which depends on the machine. Doubling the input size might double the work, or quadruple it, or barely change it. Big-O is shorthand for that growth rate, like saying 'this takes about n-squared steps' while ignoring fussy details.
depths.core: Writing f(n) = O(g(n)) means: for large enough n, f grows no faster than g, ignoring constant multipliers (the formal definition: f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for some constant c once n passes some threshold). Companion notations Ω (a lower bound) and Θ (a tight bound, both upper and lower) describe matching floors and ceilings. This abstraction lets us rank algorithms by growth rate — O(log n) ≪ O(n) ≪ O(n log n) ≪ O(n^2) ≪ O(2^n) — independent of hardware and constant factors. ('log n' grows extremely slowly; '2^n' grows explosively.)
depths.deep: Asymptotic analysis can mislead when constants or lower-order terms dominate at realistic input sizes (e.g. 'galactic algorithms' with beautiful big-O but absurdly large hidden constants). Amortized and average-case analysis refine the worst-case picture; the gap between worst-case and typical-case behavior is exactly why the simplex method and quicksort thrive in practice despite poor worst cases.

atoms.note: Memorize the ladder: constant ≪ logarithmic ≪ linear ≪ n log n ≪ quadratic ≪ exponential. Crossing from polynomial to exponential is the practical wall.

quiz.prompt: Is 3n^2 + 100n + 7 equal to O(n^2)? Justify briefly.
quiz.answer: Yes; for large n the n^2 term dominates and the whole expression is bounded by c·n^2 (e.g., c = 4) for n beyond some n_0.

quiz.prompt: What do Ω and Θ denote relative to O?
quiz.answer: Ω is an asymptotic lower bound and Θ is a tight bound (both upper and lower), whereas O is an upper bound.

atoms.title: Divide and conquer
atoms.summary: Split a problem into smaller subproblems, solve them recursively, and combine — the recipe behind mergesort and fast multiplication.

depths.eli5: Take a big job, cut it into smaller pieces, solve each piece the exact same way (cutting those further until they're trivial), then stitch the partial answers back together. Sorting a shuffled deck by splitting it in half, sorting each half, then merging the two sorted halves is the classic example ('mergesort').
depths.core: A divide-and-conquer algorithm breaks an input of size n into 'a' subproblems each of size n/b, solves them by 'recursion' (calling itself on the smaller pieces), and spends f(n) extra work combining the results — giving the recurrence (self-referential cost formula) T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n). The 'Master Theorem' solves such recurrences by comparing the combine cost f(n) to n^(log_b a); whichever term is bigger sets the overall running time. Mergesort (a=2, b=2, f(n)=n) comes out to Θ(n log n).
depths.deep: Divide and conquer wins when the subproblems are independent and recombining is cheap compared to the split. Karatsuba multiplication beats grade-school O(n^2) by cleverly reducing four sub-multiplications to three (T(n)=3T(n/2)+O(n) → O(n^1.585)); the Fast Fourier Transform pushes the idea to O(n log n) polynomial multiplication. When the subproblems overlap and get re-solved, divide and conquer wastes work and dynamic programming is the right tool instead.

atoms.title: Dynamic programming
atoms.summary: Solve overlapping subproblems once and reuse the answers, turning exponential brute force into polynomial time.

depths.eli5: If the same small subproblem keeps coming up while you work, solve it just once and jot the answer down — then look it up instead of redoing the work a thousand times. That bookkeeping is dynamic programming, and it can turn a hopelessly slow brute-force approach into a fast one.
depths.core: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has two features: 'optimal substructure' (the best overall answer is built out of best answers to subproblems) and 'overlapping subproblems' (the same subproblems come up again and again). You write a 'recurrence' (a formula expressing each case in terms of smaller cases) over a set of 'states', then either fill a table bottom-up or 'memoize' top-down (cache each result the first time you compute it) so every state is solved exactly once. Computing Fibonacci numbers, shortest paths, edit distance between strings, and the knapsack problem are canonical examples.
depths.deep: The art is choosing the right 'state space' so the recurrence is both correct and small; the running time is roughly (number of states) × (work per transition). Bellman's principle of optimality justifies the recurrence, and for shortest paths it yields the Bellman–Ford and Floyd–Warshall algorithms. Many dynamic programs can be sped up further with monotonicity tricks (convex-hull, Knuth, and divide-and-conquer optimization).

atoms.note: Two ingredients are mandatory: optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Without overlap, plain divide and conquer suffices; without optimal substructure, DP is invalid.

atoms.title: Graphs and graph search
atoms.summary: Graphs model relationships as vertices and edges; BFS and DFS explore them, underpinning shortest paths, connectivity, and ordering.

depths.eli5: A 'graph' (in this sense, not a chart) is just dots connected by lines — cities joined by roads, people joined by friendships. The dots are 'vertices' and the lines are 'edges'. To explore a graph you either fan out level by level from a starting dot (breadth-first search, BFS) or plunge deep down one path and back up when stuck (depth-first search, DFS).
depths.core: A graph G = (V, E) is a set of vertices V and a set of edges E; edges can be 'directed' (one-way) or 'undirected' (two-way), and 'weighted' (each edge has a cost) or not. Breadth-first search explores outward in layers and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; depth-first search recurses along edges and reveals connectivity, cycles, and 'topological order' (a valid ordering of tasks that respects all dependencies). Dijkstra's algorithm extends BFS to graphs with non-negative edge weights using a 'priority queue' (a structure that always hands back the smallest pending item), running in O((V+E) log V).
depths.deep: Graph problems span the whole difficulty spectrum: shortest path and minimum spanning tree are solvable in polynomial time, while Hamiltonian cycle and graph coloring are NP-complete (believed intractable). The same graph can pose an easy or a hard question — finding an Eulerian circuit (use every edge exactly once) is linear-time, but finding a Hamiltonian cycle (visit every vertex exactly once) is NP-complete, despite how similar the two sound.

quiz.prompt: Which traversal finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph, and which reveals topological order?
quiz.answer: BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS yields topological order (on a DAG).

quiz.prompt: Why can't plain BFS find shortest paths when edges have different positive weights?
quiz.answer: BFS counts edges, not weights, so a path with more low-weight edges can be cheaper than a few heavy ones; Dijkstra's priority queue handles weights.

atoms.title: Hashing and core data structures
atoms.summary: Data structures trade memory for speed; hash tables give expected O(1) lookup by scattering keys across buckets.

depths.eli5: A 'data structure' is a way of organizing information so certain operations are fast. A hash table is like a coat-check counter: a quick formula turns your ticket number into a specific hook, so the attendant grabs your coat instantly instead of checking every hook. The formula that turns a key into a slot is the 'hash function'.
depths.core: Choosing a data structure means choosing which operations you want to be fast. Arrays give O(1) lookup by position; balanced search trees give O(log n) ordered queries (find, range, sort); heaps give O(log n) access to the smallest or largest item; and hash tables give expected O(1) insert and lookup by mapping each key to a 'bucket' (slot) through a hash function. When two keys land in the same bucket — a 'collision' — it is resolved by 'chaining' (keep a small list in that bucket) or 'open addressing' (probe for the next free slot).
depths.deep: A hash table's speed guarantees are probabilistic and depend on the hash function spreading keys roughly evenly. With 'universal hashing' (picking the hash function at random from a carefully designed family) the expected number of collisions stays O(1) for any input, defeating an adversary who would otherwise craft inputs forcing the O(n) worst case. The space–time tradeoff is fundamental: Bloom filters shrink memory in exchange for occasional false positives, while cuckoo and perfect hashing buy guaranteed worst-case O(1) lookups at extra construction cost.

atoms.note: Worst-case for a naive hash table is O(n) per operation; universal/randomized hashing restores expected O(1) even against adversarial inputs.

quiz.answer: Expected O(1); worst case O(n) (all keys colliding), mitigated by universal hashing.

atoms.title: The class P (efficient computation)
atoms.summary: P is the class of problems a deterministic machine solves in polynomial time — the standard formal notion of 'tractable'.

depths.eli5: P is the collection of problems a computer can solve reasonably fast. 'Fast' here means the work grows like the input size raised to some fixed power (n, n-squared, n-cubed…) rather than exploding. A 'decision problem' is one with a yes/no answer, like 'is this number prime?'.
depths.core: A decision problem is in P if some deterministic Turing machine decides it in time O(n^k) for some constant power k ('polynomial time'). Polynomial time is the robust dividing line between 'tractable' (practically solvable) and 'intractable': it is closed under composition (plugging one efficient algorithm into another stays efficient) and stays the same across all reasonable machine models (the Cobham–Edmonds thesis), so 'polynomial' means the same thing whether you count tape steps or laptop operations.
depths.deep: Polynomial time is a deliberate idealization — an O(n^100) algorithm is 'efficient' in theory but useless in practice, while a few exponential-time algorithms run fine on real inputs. Yet the polynomial/exponential boundary stays the right theoretical cut because it is model-independent and composition-stable, which finer constant-sensitive definitions are not. Sorting, shortest paths, and primality testing all sit comfortably inside P.

quiz.prompt: Define the complexity class P.
quiz.answer: Decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the input size.

quiz.prompt: Why is 'polynomial time' the chosen line for tractability despite O(n^100) being impractical?
quiz.answer: It is robust — model-independent and closed under composition — whereas constant-sensitive definitions are not; the polynomial/exponential gap is the stable theoretical boundary.

atoms.title: The class NP and verification
atoms.summary: NP is the class of problems whose 'yes' answers have short certificates checkable in polynomial time.

depths.eli5: NP problems are ones where finding the answer might be very hard, but checking a proposed answer is fast — like a completed jigsaw puzzle: hard to assemble from scratch, but you can glance at a finished one and instantly see it's right.
depths.core: A problem is in NP if every yes-instance comes with a 'certificate' (also called a 'witness') — a short piece of evidence, polynomial in size — that a deterministic 'verifier' can check in polynomial time. Equivalently, NP is the set of problems a nondeterministic Turing machine (one allowed to 'guess' and explore many paths at once) can decide in polynomial time. P ⊆ NP, because if you can solve a problem outright you can certainly verify a claimed answer; whether that inclusion is strict (whether some NP problems truly cannot be solved as fast as they can be checked) is the famous P vs NP question.
depths.deep: NP is fundamentally about the asymmetry between finding a solution and checking one. The complementary class co-NP concerns short certificates for no-instances; whether NP = co-NP is open and tied to whether short proofs of unsatisfiability always exist. Most natural search problems whose solutions are easy to recognize but seemingly require search — Boolean satisfiability (SAT), finding a large clique, scheduling — live in NP.

atoms.note: P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXP. Each inclusion is believed strict; only P ⊊ EXP is currently proven (by the time hierarchy theorem).

quiz.prompt: Give the verifier-based definition of NP.
quiz.answer: Problems whose yes-instances have polynomial-size certificates checkable by a deterministic verifier in polynomial time.

quiz.prompt: Why is P ⊆ NP immediate?
quiz.answer: If you can solve a problem in polynomial time, you can verify any claimed answer in polynomial time (just re-solve), so every P problem is in NP.

atoms.title: Polynomial-time reductions
atoms.summary: A reduction transforms one problem into another in polynomial time, transferring tractability and hardness between them.

depths.eli5: A 'reduction' is a way of rewriting one problem as another. If you can quickly rewrite every instance of problem A as an instance of problem B, then any solver for B automatically solves A too — just translate, solve, and translate back. That means A is 'no harder than' B.
depths.core: A polynomial-time 'many-one reduction' from A to B is a polynomial-time function f that converts each instance of A into an instance of B with the very same yes/no answer, written A ≤_p B. It certifies that A is no harder than B up to polynomial factors: if B ∈ P then A ∈ P, and (taking the contrapositive) if A is known to be hard then B must be hard too. Reductions are, in effect, the algebra of computational difficulty.
depths.deep: Reductions are 'transitive' — A ≤_p B and B ≤_p C together give A ≤_p C — which is what lets a single hard problem certify the hardness of thousands of others. The direction matters: to prove B is hard you reduce a known-hard A to B (A ≤_p B), not the reverse, a very common student pitfall. 'Turing reductions' (which allow repeated oracle calls to B) are more permissive than many-one reductions and define different notions of completeness.

quiz.prompt: To prove problem B is hard, which direction of reduction do you use, and why?
quiz.answer: Reduce a known-hard problem A to B (A ≤_p B): if B were easy, A would be too, contradicting A's hardness — so B must be hard.

quiz.prompt: If A ≤_p B and B ∈ P, what follows about A?
quiz.answer: A ∈ P — tractability transfers from B back to A through the reduction.

atoms.title: NP-completeness and Cook–Levin
atoms.summary: The NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP; Boolean satisfiability was the first, and a fast algorithm for any one would crack them all.

depths.eli5: Some NP problems are universal keys: solve any one of them quickly and you'd automatically solve every NP problem quickly. SAT — deciding whether a logical formula full of ANDs, ORs, and NOTs can be made true by some setting of its variables — was the very first such universal problem found.
depths.core: A problem is 'NP-complete' if it is in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time (this second condition alone is called 'NP-hard'). The Cook–Levin theorem proved Boolean satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete by encoding the entire run of a nondeterministic machine as one big Boolean formula. Karp then showed dozens of natural problems — 3-SAT, clique, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, knapsack — are NP-complete by reducing SAT to them. A polynomial-time algorithm for any single NP-complete problem would place all of NP inside P.
depths.deep: NP-completeness explains why thousands of practically important problems all resist efficient solution: they are really the 'same' problem in disguise, linked by a web of reductions tracing back to SAT. This is why P vs NP is the central open question — proving P ≠ NP would confirm these problems are genuinely intractable, while proving P = NP would collapse the distinction and break most modern cryptography. In practice, discovering a problem is NP-hard is the signal to switch to approximation algorithms, heuristics, or special tractable cases.

atoms.note: P vs NP carries a $1M Clay Millennium Prize. Almost all experts conjecture P ≠ NP, but no proof exists.

atoms.title: Space complexity and PSPACE
atoms.summary: Measuring memory instead of time gives the classes L, PSPACE, and the theorem that nondeterministic and deterministic space coincide up to squaring.

depths.eli5: Besides 'how long does it take?', we can ask 'how much scratch paper does it need?'. That's space complexity. Some problems are gentle on memory but slow to run, and others are quick but memory-hungry — time and space are two different costs.
depths.core: Space complexity counts how many work-tape cells (scratch memory) a machine uses, regardless of how long it runs. 'PSPACE' is the class of problems solvable in polynomial space (with no limit on time); it contains NP and exactly matches the difficulty of polynomial-space games and 'quantified Boolean formulas' (the problem TQBF is PSPACE-complete). Savitch's theorem shows that for space, nondeterminism barely helps: nondeterministic space s can be simulated in deterministic space s^2 (NSPACE(s) ⊆ DSPACE(s^2)), so PSPACE = NPSPACE.
depths.deep: Memory is reusable (you can overwrite scratch paper) in a way that elapsed time is not, which is why nondeterminism is far weaker for space (Savitch) than it is believed to be for time (P vs NP). The chain L ⊆ NL ⊆ P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXP has every inclusion conjectured to be strict, yet only L ⊊ PSPACE and P ⊊ EXP are actually proven (via the space and time hierarchy theorems). The huge gaps we still cannot separate are the frontier of complexity theory.

quiz.prompt: What does Savitch's theorem say about nondeterministic vs deterministic space?
quiz.answer: NSPACE(s) ⊆ DSPACE(s^2): nondeterminism saves at most a squaring in space, so PSPACE = NPSPACE.

quiz.prompt: Why is nondeterminism much less powerful for space than it seems to be for time?
quiz.answer: Space can be reused/overwritten, so a deterministic machine can systematically search all nondeterministic paths with only quadratic extra space — no analogous trick is known for time.

atoms.title: Propositional logic
atoms.summary: Propositional logic combines true/false statements with connectives; truth tables decide validity by enumerating cases.

depths.eli5: Take simple statements that are each either true or false, and glue them together with AND, OR, NOT, and 'if…then'. A 'truth table' lists every possible combination of true/false for the parts and shows when the whole glued-together statement comes out true.
depths.core: Propositional logic builds formulas from 'atomic propositions' (basic true/false statements) and 'connectives': ¬ (not), ∧ (and), ∨ (or), → (if…then), ↔ (if and only if). An 'assignment' is a choice of true/false for each atom. A formula is 'satisfiable' if some assignment makes it true, 'valid' (a 'tautology') if every assignment makes it true, and a 'contradiction' if none does. Truth tables settle all of these by brute force over 2^n rows. Deciding satisfiability of such formulas is exactly the SAT problem at the root of NP-completeness.
depths.deep: Propositional logic is 'sound and complete': a formula is provable in a proper proof system if and only if it is a tautology — syntactic provability and semantic truth coincide. It is also 'decidable', since truth tables always terminate — precisely the property predicate (first-order) logic loses. 'Normal forms' (CNF, conjunctive normal form; DNF, disjunctive normal form) standardize formulas, and converting to CNF is the gateway to SAT solvers and the resolution proof method.

atoms.title: Predicate (first-order) logic
atoms.summary: First-order logic adds quantifiers and predicates over objects, gaining the expressive power to formalize mathematics — at the cost of decidability.

depths.eli5: Propositional logic only handles whole true/false statements. First-order logic adds the ability to say 'for all x…' and 'there exists an x…', and to talk about properties of objects and relationships between them. That extra power is enough to write down essentially all of mathematics.
depths.core: First-order (predicate) logic extends propositional logic with 'variables' that range over a 'domain' of objects, 'predicates' (properties and relations, like 'x is even' or 'x < y'), 'functions', and the 'quantifiers' ∀ ('for all') and ∃ ('there exists'). It is expressive enough to state the axioms of arithmetic, set theory, and most of mathematics. Gödel's completeness theorem shows its proof system is sound and complete: a sentence is provable exactly when it is true in every 'model' (every way of interpreting the symbols).
depths.deep: Validity in first-order logic is 'undecidable' (proved by Church and Turing) but 'recursively enumerable' — you can mechanically list all proofs, yet you cannot always decide that a non-valid sentence is non-valid. This is the precise boundary: propositional logic is decidable, first-order logic is only semi-decidable. Do not confuse the completeness theorem (provable = universally true) with the incompleteness theorems, which are about specific theories like arithmetic being unable to prove all their own truths.

atoms.note: Don't conflate Gödel's completeness theorem (about first-order logic's proof system) with his incompleteness theorems (about sufficiently strong arithmetic theories) — they point in opposite directions.

atoms.title: Proof systems and soundness/completeness
atoms.summary: A proof system is a set of axioms and inference rules; soundness means it proves only truths, completeness that it proves all of them.

depths.eli5: A proof system is a rulebook for deriving new true statements from ones you already accept. A good rulebook has two virtues: it never lets you derive something false ('sound'), and it can eventually reach every truth in its world ('complete').
depths.core: A formal proof system specifies 'axioms' (statements taken as given) and 'inference rules' (like modus ponens: from 'A' and 'if A then B', conclude 'B') that mechanically generate 'theorems' (derived statements). 'Soundness' means every provable statement is actually true (no false theorems can be derived); 'completeness' means every true statement can be proved. Natural deduction, sequent calculus, and resolution are different but equivalent proof systems for first-order logic, all sound and complete for it.
depths.deep: 'Proof complexity' asks not whether a proof exists but how long it must be: the resolution method requires exponentially long proofs for some unsatisfiable formulas (such as the pigeonhole principle), and whether short propositional proofs always exist is the open NP =? co-NP question. The Curry–Howard correspondence reveals a deep identity — proofs are programs and propositions are types — unifying logic and computation, so that constructing a proof is literally the same act as writing a program.

atoms.title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
atoms.summary: Any consistent, sufficiently strong formal system cannot prove all true statements about arithmetic, nor prove its own consistency.

depths.eli5: Any logical rulebook powerful enough to do ordinary arithmetic contains true statements it can never prove from its own rules. Worse, such a rulebook can't even prove that it will never contradict itself. Truth, it turns out, always reaches a little beyond what any fixed set of rules can capture.
depths.core: Gödel's first incompleteness theorem: any 'consistent' (never proves a contradiction), 'effectively axiomatized' (its axioms can be mechanically listed) theory strong enough to encode arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. The construction uses 'Gödel numbering' (assigning numbers to statements) to encode the sentence 'this very statement is unprovable' as a statement about arithmetic — a self-reference that is true precisely because it is unprovable. The second theorem says such a system cannot prove its own consistency, unless it is in fact inconsistent.
depths.deep: The incompleteness theorems are tightly tied to undecidability: the unprovability of certain truths mirrors the halting problem's undecidability, and Chaitin recast incompleteness using Kolmogorov complexity (no formal system can prove that a specific string's complexity exceeds the system's own size). The lesson is not that mathematics is broken but that truth outruns proof in any fixed formal system — there is no finite set of axioms that captures every arithmetic truth.

atoms.note: First theorem: truth > provability. Second theorem: a consistent system can't certify its own consistency. Both require the system to be strong enough to do arithmetic.

atoms.title: One-way functions
atoms.summary: A one-way function is easy to compute but computationally hard to invert — the conjectured bedrock of modern cryptography.

depths.eli5: Some operations are like scrambling an egg: easy to do, practically impossible to undo. A 'one-way function' is the mathematical version — quick to compute forwards, but so hard to reverse that nobody can in any reasonable time. Cryptography is built on functions like that.
depths.core: A one-way function f can be computed in polynomial time, but no efficient algorithm can find a 'preimage' (an input x that produces a given output f(x)) for random x, except with negligible probability. Whether such functions even exist is unproven, and their existence would imply P ≠ NP — yet they are both necessary and sufficient for most of cryptography: secure encryption, digital signatures, and pseudorandom generators all rest on them. Leading candidates are built on integer factoring and the discrete-logarithm problem.
depths.deep: Cryptography depends on 'average-case' hardness, not merely 'worst-case': NP-hardness only guarantees that some instances are hard, but cryptography needs a function that is hard on typical, randomly chosen inputs. One-way functions formalize exactly that. They also connect to pseudorandomness — a function whose output no efficient test can tell apart from random is the engine behind stream ciphers — and to Shannon's distinction between 'unconditional' (information-theoretic) and 'computational' security: a one-time pad is unbreakable in principle, while practical crypto trades that ideal for keys you can actually distribute.

atoms.note: The existence of one-way functions is the single most important open assumption in cryptography; it implies P ≠ NP but is believed to be strictly stronger.

atoms.title: Public-key cryptography
atoms.summary: Public-key systems use a publishable encryption key and a secret decryption key, enabling secure communication without sharing secrets first.

depths.eli5: Imagine handing out copies of an open padlock to everyone, while keeping the only key for yourself. Anyone can snap a box shut with your padlock, but only you can open it. That's public-key cryptography: strangers can send you secrets without ever meeting to agree on a shared password first.
depths.core: Public-key (also called 'asymmetric') cryptography gives each person two matched keys: a 'public key' shared openly and a 'private key' kept secret. Anyone can encrypt a message with your public key, but only you, holding the private key, can decrypt it; swapping the roles produces 'digital signatures' (proof a message came from you). RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring large integers; Diffie–Hellman and elliptic-curve systems rely on the discrete-logarithm problem — these are 'trapdoor one-way functions' (one-way unless you hold the secret trapdoor).
depths.deep: The breakthrough (Diffie–Hellman in 1976, then RSA) solved the key-distribution problem that had crippled older 'symmetric' crypto: two parties can now agree on a shared secret over a fully public channel. The security is computational and conditional — Shor's algorithm can factor integers and compute discrete logs in polynomial time on a large quantum computer, threatening RSA and elliptic-curve crypto (ECC) and driving the shift to 'post-quantum cryptography' based on lattice problems believed hard even for quantum machines.

atoms.title: Pseudorandomness
atoms.summary: A pseudorandom generator stretches a short seed into a long string no efficient test can distinguish from true randomness.

depths.eli5: Start with a tiny bit of genuine randomness (a 'seed'), then run it through a clever recipe that spits out a long stream of bits. To anyone without unlimited computing power, that stream looks completely random — even though it's totally determined by the seed. It isn't truly random, but no fast test can catch the difference.
depths.core: A 'pseudorandom generator' (PRG) is an algorithm that turns a short truly-random seed into a much longer output that is 'computationally indistinguishable' from genuinely uniform random bits — meaning no efficient (polynomial-time) test can tell the two apart with any meaningful advantage. PRGs are known to exist if one-way functions do (the Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby theorem). They power stream ciphers, simulations, and 'derandomization', letting you replace scarce true randomness with cheap pseudorandom bits.
depths.deep: Pseudorandomness is randomness relative to an observer's computational power: a PRG's output has low Kolmogorov complexity (a short program generates it) yet is operationally random to any bounded adversary — showing that 'random' is not absolute but resource-relative. The derandomization conjectures (that BPP = P, assuming strong circuit lower bounds) suggest true randomness may give no extra computational power at all, only convenience.

atoms.title: PAC learning
atoms.summary: PAC learning formalizes learning from examples: with high probability, output a hypothesis that is approximately correct on unseen data.

depths.eli5: Learning from examples works like this: you see a pile of labeled examples (this photo is a cat, that one isn't), then you guess a rule. A good rule is mostly right on brand-new examples you've never seen — and you want to be confident that it really is mostly right. PAC learning makes that intuition precise.
depths.core: In Valiant's 'Probably Approximately Correct' (PAC) framework, a 'concept class' (a family of possible rules) is PAC-learnable if some algorithm can, for any target rule and any unknown distribution of examples, draw a polynomial number of samples and output — with probability at least 1 − δ — a 'hypothesis' (its guessed rule) whose error is at most ε. The two knobs separate accuracy (ε, the 'approximately') from confidence (δ, the 'probably'). The whole point is generalizing from finite data, not memorizing it.
depths.deep: PAC makes a 'distribution-free' demand: the learner must succeed no matter what distribution generates the examples, which is what makes the guarantee meaningful. The key insight is that generalization is possible only if the hypothesis class is restricted — an unrestricted learner can always fit the training data perfectly yet behave arbitrarily on new points ('overfitting'). Exactly how much restriction is needed is captured by the VC dimension.

quiz.prompt: Why must the hypothesis class be restricted for learning to generalize?

atoms.title: VC dimension
atoms.summary: The VC dimension measures a model's capacity by the largest set of points it can label in every possible way — it sets the sample size needed to learn.

depths.eli5: A model's 'power' (its capacity) is the size of the biggest set of points it can fit perfectly no matter how you label them — every yes/no combination. More power sounds good, but it means you need more examples before you can trust the model on data it hasn't seen. The VC dimension is the number that measures this power.
depths.core: A hypothesis class 'shatters' a set of points if, for every possible way of labeling them (every assignment of yes/no), some hypothesis in the class produces exactly that labeling. The 'VC dimension' (named for Vapnik and Chervonenkis) is the size of the largest set the class can shatter. A class is PAC-learnable if and only if its VC dimension is finite, and the number of examples needed (the 'sample complexity') scales roughly as Θ((d/ε) + (1/ε)log(1/δ)) where d is the VC dimension — capacity directly sets how much data you need.
depths.deep: VC dimension quantifies the 'bias–variance tradeoff': high capacity can fit almost anything (low bias) but demands far more data to generalize (high variance), formalizing Occam's razor — simpler classes generalize from fewer examples. Concretely, axis-aligned half-lines on the number line have VC dimension 1, intervals 2, and straight-line ('linear') separators in d-dimensional space have VC dimension d+1. A class that can shatter arbitrarily large sets (infinite VC dimension) is not PAC-learnable at all.

atoms.note: Finite VC dimension is exactly the condition for distribution-free PAC learnability — the fundamental theorem of statistical learning.

atoms.title: Entropy bridges information and statistical mechanics
atoms.summary: Shannon's information entropy and Boltzmann/Gibbs thermodynamic entropy are the same functional, linking bits to physical energy.

depths.eli5: Physicists measure 'disorder' in a box of gas; information theorists measure 'uncertainty' in a message. It turns out these are the very same formula, just written with different units. The bits in your phone and the heat in a gas are governed by one shared idea — entropy.
depths.core: The 'Gibbs entropy' of physics, S = −k_B Σ p_i ln p_i (where k_B is Boltzmann's constant and ln is the natural log), and the Shannon entropy H = −Σ p_i log2 p_i of information theory are the same function, differing only by the constant k_B and the choice of logarithm base. Jaynes recast statistical mechanics as 'inference': the equilibrium state of a physical system is the maximum-entropy probability distribution consistent with what you know (such as the average energy), recovering the famous Boltzmann distribution as the least-biased guess. Landauer's principle then attaches a real physical energy cost, k_B T ln 2, to erasing a single bit.
depths.deep: This identification turns thermodynamics into a special case of information theory: temperature plays the role of a Lagrange multiplier on the energy constraint, and the partition function is just a normalizer. Landauer's bound — together with Bennett's resolution of the Maxwell's-demon paradox — shows that information is physical: logically irreversible erasure must dissipate heat, closing the loop between computation, entropy, and the second law of thermodynamics. The same maximum-entropy principle reappears in machine learning as the logistic/softmax model and in statistics as the exponential families.

atoms.note: Landauer's principle: erasing one bit costs at least k_B T ln 2 ≈ 0.018 eV of dissipated energy at room temperature — the thermodynamic price of forgetting.

atoms.title: Modern machine learning — a glimpse
atoms.summary: Deep networks fit huge parametric functions by gradient descent, and their surprising generalization stretches classical learning theory.

depths.eli5: A neural network is a giant adjustable function with millions of little knobs ('parameters'). Training nudges those knobs a tiny bit at a time to reduce its mistakes on example data. Remarkably, after enough nudging it can handle brand-new examples it never saw during training. Nobody fully understands why this works as well as it does.
depths.core: A neural network stacks layers, each a 'linear map' (a weighted sum) followed by a simple 'nonlinearity' (a bending function), into one huge function with millions or billions of parameters. Training minimizes a 'loss' (a mistake score) by 'gradient descent' — repeatedly stepping the parameters in the direction that lowers the loss. The needed gradients are computed efficiently by 'backpropagation', which is really dynamic programming reusing the calculus chain rule across layers. Classical VC theory predicts such hugely 'over-parameterized' models should overfit badly, yet they generalize well — a puzzle modern theory (implicit regularization, the 'double descent' curve) is still working to explain.
depths.deep: Backpropagation is exactly dynamic programming over the network's computation graph: each intermediate derivative is computed once and reused, so the total gradient cost is linear in network size rather than exponential. The frontier puzzle is generalization when parameters vastly outnumber the training data — classical uniform-convergence bounds (VC dimension, Rademacher complexity) become vacuous there, so model capacity alone no longer explains why learning succeeds. The information-bottleneck view and links back to statistical mechanics (energy landscapes, phase transitions in learning) are active attempts to rebuild the theory.

atoms.title: Randomized algorithms
atoms.summary: Algorithms that flip coins can be simpler and faster than deterministic ones, trading certainty for high-probability correctness or speed.

depths.eli5: Sometimes letting an algorithm flip coins and make random choices makes it faster or simpler, while still being almost always right. For example, quicksort runs fast on average when it picks a random item to split the list around, side-stepping the bad cases that trip up a fixed choice.
depths.core: Randomized algorithms consume random bits while running. 'Las Vegas' algorithms (like randomized quicksort) always return the correct answer but have a random running time; 'Monte Carlo' algorithms (like the Miller–Rabin primality test) run in a fixed time but may give a wrong answer with a small, controllable probability. Randomness often dodges worst-case 'adversarial' inputs and simplifies design. The corresponding complexity class is BPP ('bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time') — problems solvable fast with a small error chance.
depths.deep: The true power of randomness is subtle: under widely believed circuit lower bounds, BPP = P, meaning randomness buys convenience and speed but not fundamentally more solvable problems ('derandomization' via pseudorandom generators). Yet in other models randomization is provably essential — distributed consensus, communication complexity, and cryptography rely on it irreducibly. The gap between 'random helps' and 'random is necessary' depends on the model.

atoms.title: Kullback–Leibler divergence
atoms.summary: KL divergence measures the extra bits wasted when you encode data from p using a code optimized for q.

depths.eli5: Suppose you build your data compression assuming the world behaves like distribution q, but the world is actually distribution p. You'll waste some bits because your code was tuned to the wrong guess. KL divergence is exactly the count of how many extra bits you waste, on average.
depths.core: The Kullback–Leibler divergence D_KL(p‖q) is the average number of extra bits you spend by coding data from the true distribution p with a code that was optimized for a different distribution q. It is never negative (Gibbs' inequality), is zero exactly when p = q, but is 'asymmetric' (D_KL(p‖q) ≠ D_KL(q‖p)) so it is not a true distance metric. Mutual information is the special case D_KL(joint distribution ‖ product of the separate distributions), and 'cross-entropy' equals entropy plus KL divergence.
depths.deep: KL divergence is the natural 'distance' from a model to reality in 'information geometry', and minimizing it is exactly maximum-likelihood estimation — fitting a model to data minimizes D_KL(empirical data ‖ model). Its asymmetry encodes a real modeling choice: D_KL(p‖q) punishes q for assigning low probability where p is high ('mode-covering'), while D_KL(q‖p) does the reverse ('mode-seeking') — a distinction that shapes variational inference and generative models.

atoms.note: Cross-entropy loss, ubiquitous in machine learning, is entropy plus KL divergence — minimizing it fits the model distribution to the data distribution.

atoms.title: Conditional probability and Bayes' rule
atoms.summary: Bayes' rule inverts conditional probabilities, updating a prior belief into a posterior in light of evidence.

depths.eli5: Bayes' rule flips a 'how likely is the evidence?' question into a 'how likely is the cause?' question. If you know how often a test beeps when someone truly has a disease, Bayes lets you compute how likely they actually have the disease once the test beeps — combining the test with how rare the disease is to begin with.
depths.core: 'Conditional probability' P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) is the probability that A happens given that B has occurred (P(A∩B) is the chance both happen). Bayes' rule rearranges this into P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A)/P(B), letting you invert a known 'likelihood' P(B|A) into the 'posterior' P(A|B) you want, using your 'prior' belief P(A). It is the engine of all probabilistic inference, from spam filters to medical diagnosis.
depths.deep: The 'base-rate fallacy' is Bayes' rule ignored: a rare condition (small prior) combined with an imperfect test makes most positive results false positives, no matter how 'accurate' the test sounds. Bayesian updating is also the discrete cousin of the maximum-entropy / inference view of statistical mechanics — both treat probability as a state of knowledge updated by constraints, not as a property of the world alone.

atoms.note: P(B) in the denominator is the normalizer, expandable via the law of total probability: P(B) = Σ_A P(B|A)P(A).

atoms.title: Regular expressions
atoms.summary: Regular expressions are an algebraic notation for patterns, exactly as expressive as finite automata.

depths.eli5: A 'regular expression' (regex) is a compact written pattern — like 'one or more digits' or 'a word starting with cat' — that a machine can test text against. It can describe exactly the same patterns that a simple state-hopping machine (a finite automaton) can recognize.
depths.core: Regular expressions are built from three operations on patterns: 'union' (written |, meaning 'this or that'), 'concatenation' (one pattern followed by another), and the 'Kleene star' (zero-or-more repetitions), starting from single symbols and the empty string. Kleene's theorem proves they describe exactly the 'regular languages' — every regex can be converted into an equivalent NFA, and every DFA back into a regex. They are the everyday practical front-end to finite automata in text processing.
depths.deep: The Kleene star is what lets a finite written pattern match strings of unbounded length, and it corresponds precisely to a loop (a revisited state) in the automaton. Real-world regex engines often add 'backreferences' (matching a repeat of something matched earlier), which push them beyond truly regular into a strictly more powerful — and worst-case exponential — regime, a frequent source of 'catastrophic backtracking' denial-of-service bugs (ReDoS).

quiz.answer: Kleene's theorem: regular expressions describe exactly the regular languages, equivalently those recognized by finite automata.

quiz.prompt: Why can a regex engine with backreferences behave worse than linear time?
quiz.answer: Backreferences exceed regular expressiveness, forcing backtracking search that can blow up exponentially — the catastrophic-backtracking ReDoS pitfall.

atoms.title: Greedy algorithms
atoms.summary: Greedy algorithms make the locally best choice at each step, which yields a global optimum only when the problem has matroid-like structure.

depths.eli5: A greedy algorithm always grabs the best-looking option right now and never reconsiders. Sometimes that string of locally-best choices happens to land you the best overall answer; other times it walks you into a dead end. The trick is knowing which problems it's safe on.
depths.core: A greedy algorithm builds a solution one step at a time, each step taking whatever choice looks best at that moment. This is guaranteed correct only when the problem has the 'greedy-choice property' (a locally best choice can always be extended to a globally best solution) and 'optimal substructure'. Minimum spanning tree (Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms), Huffman coding, and interval scheduling are classic greedy successes; the general 0/1 knapsack problem is the classic failure.
depths.deep: The deep reason greedy works for minimum spanning tree but not knapsack is 'matroid theory': greedy is provably optimal exactly on problems whose feasible solutions form a matroid (an abstract structure capturing 'independence'). When greedy fails, dynamic programming or exchange arguments are needed. Even when greedy is not optimal, it often guarantees a fixed 'approximation ratio', making it a workhorse for NP-hard problems.

atoms.title: Amortized analysis
atoms.summary: Amortized analysis bounds the average cost per operation over a sequence, even when individual operations are occasionally expensive.

depths.eli5: Some operations are usually cheap but every so often very expensive. Instead of judging by the rare expensive one, amortized analysis spreads that big cost across all the cheap ones to find the true average cost per operation over a whole run.
depths.core: Amortized analysis measures the average cost of an operation across a worst-case sequence of operations, rather than the cost of the single worst operation. For example, a 'dynamic array' that doubles its capacity when full costs O(n) on the rare resize but only O(1) 'amortized' per insertion, because resizes happen rarely enough that their total cost is spread thin. The three standard proof techniques are the aggregate method, the accounting (banker's) method, and the potential method.
depths.deep: Amortized is not the same as average-case: it makes no probabilistic assumption and holds for every worst-case sequence. The 'potential method' assigns the data structure a 'stored energy' Φ; the amortized cost of an operation is its actual cost plus the change ΔΦ, so cheap operations bank potential that expensive ones later spend. This makes data structures like splay trees and Fibonacci heaps analyzable despite wild swings in their per-operation cost.

atoms.note: Amortized O(1) per op over n ops means total O(n) — distinct from, and stronger than, an average-case probabilistic claim.

atoms.title: The time hierarchy theorem
atoms.summary: More time strictly buys more computational power: there are problems solvable in O(n^3) time but not in O(n^2).

depths.eli5: Give a computer genuinely more running time and it can genuinely solve more problems — no surprise, but here it's actually proven, not just assumed. It's one of the few clean, settled facts in complexity theory, where most of the big questions are still open.
depths.core: The time hierarchy theorem says that if you allow a time budget f that grows enough faster than another budget g (for well-behaved 'time-constructible' bounds), then DTIME(g) ⊊ DTIME(f): strictly more time lets you decide strictly more problems. The proof uses 'diagonalization' — it builds a machine that, given the extra time, deliberately disagrees with the output of every machine confined to less time, so it can't be in the smaller class. This is exactly why P ⊊ EXP (problems solvable in polynomial time are a strict subset of those solvable in exponential time) is a proven theorem, not merely a conjecture.
depths.deep: The hierarchy theorems are among the rare 'unconditional' separations in complexity theory, and they work because the diagonalization can be carried out within the allotted time/space budget. Crucially, diagonalization alone cannot resolve P vs NP: the 'relativization' barrier (the Baker–Gill–Solovay result) shows that any proof technique blind to a machine's internals fails on P vs NP, which is why that question stays open while the hierarchy theorems are settled.

atoms.note: Hierarchy theorems give us our only proven separations (P ⊊ EXP, L ⊊ PSPACE); the famous open separations (P vs NP) provably need non-relativizing techniques.

atoms.title: Lossy compression and rate–distortion
atoms.equation: R(D)=\min_{p(\hat x\mid x):\,\mathbb{E}[d]\le D} I(X;\hat X)
atoms.summary: Rate–distortion theory gives the minimum number of bits needed to represent a source within an allowed level of distortion.

depths.eli5: Perfect, lossless compression can only shrink a file so far. But if you're willing to lose a little quality — a slightly blurrier photo, a slightly rougher song — you can use far fewer bits. Rate–distortion theory tells you the best possible trade between file size and faithfulness.
depths.core: Lossless coding is bounded below by entropy, but allowing some 'distortion' D (a measured amount of error in the reconstruction) lets you compress further. The 'rate–distortion function' R(D) is the smallest bit rate you can achieve while keeping the average distortion at or below D. Formally it is the minimum mutual information I(X;X̂) between the source X and its reconstruction X̂, over all reconstructions meeting the distortion limit. It is the 'lossy' counterpart of the source coding theorem and the theoretical floor underneath JPEG, MP3, and video codecs.
depths.deep: R(D) is convex and decreasing: R(0) recovers the entropy (perfect, lossless reconstruction), and R climbs steeply as you demand near-perfect fidelity. The curve formalizes the universal engineering trade-off between file size and quality. Rate–distortion is also the conceptual ancestor of the 'information bottleneck' in deep learning, which compresses an input while preserving the information relevant to a target — relevance-constrained lossy coding.

atoms.title: Approximation algorithms
atoms.summary: When a problem is NP-hard, approximation algorithms find provably near-optimal solutions in polynomial time.

depths.eli5: When finding the perfect answer is too slow to be practical, settle for one that's guaranteed to be close — say, provably never worse than twice the best possible — but that you can find quickly. That guarantee of closeness is what separates an approximation algorithm from a random guess.
depths.core: An α-approximation algorithm runs in polynomial time and always returns a solution within a factor of α of the optimal value (for example, a 2-approximation is never more than twice as costly as the best answer). For NP-hard optimization problems this is the practical response to intractability: vertex cover has a simple 2-approximation, set cover a (ln n)-approximation, and some problems admit a PTAS (a polynomial-time approximation scheme, getting arbitrarily close to optimal). The best achievable α is itself a deep question, tied to 'hardness of approximation'.
depths.deep: The PCP theorem reveals that for some problems even approximating is NP-hard: there is a threshold ratio below which no polynomial-time algorithm can go unless P = NP (e.g., MAX-3SAT is hard to approximate beyond 7/8). So NP-hardness comes in grades — some problems approximate arbitrarily well (PTAS), some to a fixed constant, and some not at all — refining the coarse P-vs-NP picture into a rich landscape of approximability.

atoms.note: Hardness of approximation (via the PCP theorem) shows some problems are not just hard to solve exactly but provably hard to even approximate beyond a fixed ratio.

atoms.title: Typical sequences and the AEP
atoms.summary: For long sequences of i.i.d. symbols, almost all probability concentrates on roughly 2^{nH} nearly-equiprobable 'typical' sequences.

depths.eli5: Flip a biased coin a million times and the exact sequence you get is almost certainly one of a fairly predictable family — the 'typical' outcomes, the ones with roughly the expected mix of heads and tails. There are about 2 raised to the power (length × entropy) of these typical sequences, and nearly all the probability lives among them.
depths.core: The 'asymptotic equipartition property' (AEP) is the information-theoretic version of the law of large numbers. For a sequence of 'i.i.d.' symbols (independent and identically distributed — each drawn the same way, independently), as the length n grows the per-symbol log-probability converges to the entropy H(X). As a result, almost all of the probability concentrates on a 'typical set' of about 2^{nH} sequences, each of probability near 2^{-nH}. This is the precise reason that H bits per symbol are enough for compression: you only need to give index numbers to the typical set.
depths.deep: The AEP is what makes Shannon's source and channel coding theorems provable: compression hands short codes only to the typical sequences (ignoring the vanishingly rare atypical ones), and channel coding picks codewords so that their typical outputs barely overlap. The exponential gap between the 2^{nH} typical sequences and the |alphabet|^n total possible sequences is the quantitative heart of why information can be compressed at all.

atoms.note: Typical set size ≈ 2^{nH}; total sequence count = |X|^n. Compression works because the typical set is exponentially smaller whenever H < log|X|.
